pharm: Insulin secretagogue; closes pancreatic beta-cell ATP-sensitive potassium (K-ATP) channels
quick: Standard-release 40-320 mg/day; MR 30-120 mg once daily
Take with meals (standard) or with breakfast (MR)
summary: Gliclazide is a second-generation sulfonylurea used in type 2 diabetes mellitus to lower blood glucose by stimulating endogenous insulin secretion. It is available as standard-release and modified-release (MR) formulations. The principal risk is hypoglycaemia, particularly in the elderly and in renal or hepatic impairment.
indications: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (non-insulin-dependent) when diet, exercise, and weight reduction are insufficient

dosage.d: Initial 40-80 mg daily; usual range 40-320 mg/day; doses above 160 mg/day in divided doses
dosage.t: Once daily or divided with meals
dosage.n: Titrate to glycaemic response; take with meals

dosage.d: Initial 30 mg once daily; range 30-120 mg once daily
dosage.n: Adjust at intervals of at least 1 month; max 120 mg/day

admin: Swallow tablets whole with water; do not chew or crush MR tablets
Take standard-release doses with meals to reduce hypoglycaemia risk
Take modified-release dose once daily with breakfast
Maintain consistent meal pattern and do not skip meals
Titrate dose against blood glucose and HbA1c under medical supervision
moa: Stimulates insulin release from functioning pancreatic beta cells by binding the sulfonylurea receptor (SUR1) and closing ATP-sensitive potassium channels. The resulting membrane depolarisation opens voltage-gated calcium channels, raising intracellular calcium and triggering insulin exocytosis. It also has reported effects on reducing platelet aggregation and improving microvascular function.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to gliclazide, other sulfonylureas, or sulfonamides
relative: Irregular or inadequate caloric intake / malnutrition
Mild to moderate renal or hepatic impairment
monitor: Hypoglycaemia, especially with missed meals, exertion, or alcohol
Signs of loss of glycaemic control with intercurrent illness

preg: Not recommended in pregnancy; sulfonylureas may cross the placenta and cause neonatal hypoglycaemia. Insulin is the preferred treatment for diabetes during pregnancy and gliclazide should be switched to insulin before conception or as soon as pregnancy is identified.
lact: Contraindicated during breastfeeding; in view of the risk of neonatal hypoglycaemia, gliclazide should not be used while breastfeeding. Insulin is preferred.
renal: Use with caution in mild to moderate renal impairment owing to increased hypoglycaemia risk; contraindicated in severe renal impairment. Start at the lowest dose and monitor closely.
hepatic: Use with caution and reduce dose in mild to moderate hepatic impairment; contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment. Impaired hepatic metabolism and gluconeogenesis increase hypoglycaemia risk.

major: Miconazole (systemic and oral gel) - severe hypoglycaemia, contraindicated
Insulin and other hypoglycaemic agents - additive hypoglycaemia
Alcohol - increased hypoglycaemia and disulfiram-like reaction
moderate: ACE inhibitors - may enhance glucose lowering
Corticosteroids, thiazides, danazol - reduce glycaemic control (hyperglycaemia)
minor: MAO inhibitors - may enhance hypoglycaemic effect
interactions.food: Take with food; skipping meals markedly increases hypoglycaemia risk
interactions.alcohol: Avoid; alcohol increases the risk and severity of hypoglycaemia and may cause a disulfiram-like reaction
interactions.diagnostics: Affects blood glucose and HbA1c; consider when interpreting glycaemic monitoring

serious: Severe or prolonged hypoglycaemia (may require hospitalisation)
rare: Skin and hypersensitivity reactions (rash, pruritus, urticaria)
emergency: Severe hypoglycaemia with confusion, seizures, or coma

monitoring: Full blood count if clinically indicated
counsel: Recognise and treat hypoglycaemia (sweating, tremor, confusion) with fast-acting glucose
Do not skip meals; take the dose with food as directed
Avoid alcohol, which increases the risk of low blood sugar
Swallow MR tablets whole; do not crush or chew
Carry a source of sugar and diabetes identification
Report jaundice, unusual bleeding, infection, or persistent rash
pk: Up to 24 hours (MR supports once-daily dosing)
pearls: Not FDA-approved; record based on EMA/SmPC/BNF sources; pending clinical review.
Modified-release 30 mg is approximately equivalent to standard-release 80 mg in glycaemic effect
Lower intrinsic hypoglycaemia risk than glibenclamide, but risk remains significant in the elderly and renal impairment
Largely hepatically metabolised to inactive metabolites, making it relatively suitable when renal function is impaired (with caution)
Miconazole co-administration is contraindicated due to severe hypoglycaemia risk
Hold during acute illness, surgery, or infection where insulin may be needed temporarily
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered with food if it is still well before the next scheduled dose; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the normal schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one.
overdose: Overdose causes hypoglycaemia, which may be severe and prolonged. Treat conscious patients with oral carbohydrate; severe cases require intravenous glucose (dextrose) and close monitoring, as hypoglycaemia can recur over many hours and may require admission. Glucagon may be used. Avoid prolonged use of strong glucose solutions that can cause rebound hypoglycaemia; monitor blood glucose for at least 24-48 hours.
